0.description: The extent as a WKT literal, uplifting to `geo:asWKT` with datatype `geo:wktLiteral`. An optional leading CRS URI is permitted, per GeoSPARQL; without one, CRS84 (longitude/latitude in degrees) is assumed, as GeoSPARQL specifies.
End of the period, in the same form as `startDate`.

Start of the period, as an ISO 8601 year, year-month, or date. Granularity is workflow-specific and deliberately not fixed, but the format is, so two periods stated at the same granularity compare correctly as plain string ordering.
A non-calendar, scenario-indexed temporal position, as a concept from the FOCAL scenario-markers scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). Open: other scenario indices may follow.

Which axis of variation this statement constrains, and therefore what shape `value` takes. Open vocabulary, seeded from the eight FOCAL pilot questionnaires and expected to grow; a new term needs no schema change unless it also needs a new `value` shape.

Identifier for this constraint, so a rule can cite it in `when[].constraint`. Optional only for a constraint no rule refers to.
An **IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name** (see bblocks://ogc.ogc-utils.iri-or-curie). A local name is resolved against the document's base URI and is right for a constraint specific to one workflow. An IRI or CURIE gives the constraint a **global identity**, which is what makes a boundary shareable: the EURO-CORDEX EUR-11 domain is the same extent for several FOCAL workflows, and each restating it as a private local name leaves nothing able to tell that they are the same boundary. Declaring it here under its global identifier says so.
A CURIE expands only if its prefix is declared in the JSON-LD context (via `x-jsonld-prefixes` or an imported block); an undeclared prefix is read as a URI scheme and `acme:eur11` stays `acme:eur11`, which validates and means nothing. Use a full IRI unless the prefix is known to be in scope.
Giving a constraint a global identifier makes the boundary shareable, not fetchable: it is still declared in full in every statement that cites it, so a reader always has the extent in front of them. What the identifier buys is being able to ask which workflows are bounded by this exact domain.
Which aspect of the envelope this statement describes. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.
Free-text elaboration of a transferability fact the controlled vocabularies can't capture. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment` on whatever it is attached to.

The constraint value, shaped by `dimension`:
- `spatial`/`jurisdictional` — a geometry, as `{"asWKT": "POLYGON((...))"}`. WKT rather
  than GeoJSON coordinate arrays: it uplifts to a real `geo:wktLiteral`, which is the
  form GeoSPARQL's topological functions actually operate on, it is one value rather than
  a nested array so nothing is lost or reshaped in uplift, and it is dramatically more
  compact (UP-WF2's European coverage MultiPolygon costs a few hundred characters
  instead of 1,283 lines of Turtle). An approximate extent is expected and fine — a
  published bounding box for a model domain, say — but it must be a real extent, since a
  free-text place name cannot answer the containment question this dimension exists for.
- `temporal` — either `{"startDate", "endDate"}` (a calendar span, uplifting to
  `dcat:startDate`/`dcat:endDate` on a `dcterms:PeriodOfTime`) or `{"scenarioMarker"}`
  for results that are not calendar-indexed at all. A Global Warming Level is the
  evidenced case: it is reached in different years under different emissions scenarios
  and ensemble members, so a calendar interval would be a fabrication rather than a
  simplification. Markers are concepts, not free text, so `GWL+1.5` written two ways by
  two pilots is one thing rather than two.
- `ecological`/`climatic`/anything else — a plain string. "A comparable ecological range"
  is not a place and does not become machine-checkable by being wrapped in coordinates it
  does not have. A rule may still cite such a constraint; the condition is then a
  judgement a person makes, stated in the same structure, which is honest about where
  automation stops.

properties.description: The validity envelope, as one or more role/dimension/value statements. Required: something with no stated boundary at all is not yet a portability statement, and inventing one to satisfy the schema would be worse than leaving the workflow unmodelled.
The reference and calibration artifacts this statement's rules govern, each declared once and cited by `rules[].appliesTo`. May be empty when every rule is about the workflow as a whole.

Identifier for this artifact, cited by `rules[].appliesTo`. An IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name resolved against the document base (see bblocks://ogc.ogc-utils.iri-or-curie). A shared reference dataset that several workflows depend on is worth identifying globally, for the same reason a shared envelope constraint is.
Label identifying the artifact, in the words the source used (e.g. "downscaled FOCAL climate data", "Quitt climate-zone thresholds/limits"). Uplifts to `dcterms:title` on a `prov:Entity`.

What kind of thing this artifact is, independent of whether an executable workflow description exists that could give it an identifier yet. The eight FOCAL questionnaires' artifacts are not uniformly workflow inputs: some are inputs, some are outputs later reused as another run's input (a trained model), and some never appear in an executable graph at all (physical infrastructure to be re-deployed; an optional validation reference). Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.

JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) locating the artifact inside the document this statement annotates. For the CWL profile in bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.workflow that means `/inputs/<id>` or `/outputs/<id>`, but the pointer carries no CWL assumption. Optional: meaningful only for the `workflow-input` and `workflow-output` roles, and only fillable once a real Application Package exists to point into. Omit it rather than guess.
Free-text note about the artifact. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment`.

What must happen, to which artifacts, under which conditions. **An empty array is a meaningful value**: it says the artifacts were assessed and none needs adapting, which is a positive portability fact and quite different from the property being absent, which says nobody has looked. Requiring at least one entry would force anyone in the first situation to invent a rule.

Identifiers of the artifacts this rule governs, from the enclosing statement's `artifacts`. Several artifacts may share one rule — FP-WF2's four Czechia-specific reference files do. Omit for a rule that applies to the workflow as a whole.
The conditions under which this rule fires, ANDed together. Two conditions here mean both must hold; two rules mean either suffices.

The `id` of an envelope constraint in the enclosing statement's `envelope`, written the same way it is declared there — an IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name. Whichever form is used, the constraint must still be declared in the statement, so a reader has the extent in front of them rather than a bare identifier: a global identifier makes a boundary shareable, it does not make it fetchable.

How the target is compared against that constraint. `outside` is the condition under which almost every evidenced FOCAL rule fires; `inside` states the complementary case, which is what lets a cascade be written without losing its connecting condition — UP-WF2's "reuse within the domain, otherwise substitute or fail" is two rules over the same constraint. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab, where each term also records how it is evaluated per dimension.
A coarse statement of what fires this rule, for cases where no envelope constraint can be cited precisely. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.
One or more actions, any of which resolves the rule — an OR-set, not a required combination. No evidenced case needs two applied simultaneously.

Whether applying one of `actions` is mandatory once the conditions hold. Defaults to true. When false, skipping is allowed but degrades result quality or trust rather than blocking execution — say what degrades in `transferabilityNotes`.
Named `mandatory` rather than `required`: a data property spelled like a JSON Schema keyword reads as the keyword, and this one sits beside real `required` lists.
